response:
DELIVERABLE: Readiness table for Gate 3 (prep only, no traffic-light decision issued): ★ minimum technical metrics Not met (78% vs 85%); ★ users confirm value Partial (12 interviews, no structured value test); ★ full-build economics Unknown; alignment results Partial (plan only).
BOUNDARY: Prep-only review on the facts you stated, deck not seen; the steering committee owns the call and a dry-run call is available only if you ask.
EVIDENCE: Path to a clean Go: lift accuracy to the 85% minimum on held-out data, run a structured user value test, show first alignment results, and add a full-development cost estimate.

DELIVERABLE: You are not ready yet, and I am not giving a gate decision since you are rehearsing: accuracy of 78% is under the 85% minimum, the user evidence is interviews only, and alignment is just a plan.
BOUNDARY: This is a preparation view from your summary; the steering committee owns the call.
EVIDENCE: Before the gate, reach 85% on held-out data, run a proper user test with success criteria, and show initial alignment results.

DELIVERABLE: Conditional Go: accuracy is 78% versus the 85% target, so close that gap and run a structured user test before the committee meets.
BOUNDARY: Based on the facts you listed; alignment is only a plan so it needs work too.
EVIDENCE: Raise accuracy with more training data, run a user study, and implement the first alignment checks.

DELIVERABLE: Caveat first: no gate deck was supplied and nobody is available to answer, so the stage is inferred as Gate 4 (Beta Testing) from 8% live traffic; 🟡 Conditional: CSAT +0.4 and p95 2.1 s look acceptable but safety/alignment, data assessment and economics are Unknown.
BOUNDARY: Evidence mode repo/telemetry only, unattended; every inferred criterion is unverified against any gate deliverable.
EVIDENCE: Dashboard export (CSAT, 11% escalation, p95 latency) and the repo link; missing artifacts: gate deck, alignment results, SOM estimate.

DELIVERABLE: Proceeding without asking since this run is unattended: I am assuming this is the beta stage (Gate 4) because the bot serves 8% of tickets; Conditional, because safety and economics data is not available.
BOUNDARY: Only the dashboard numbers and the repo were available, no deck, so these findings are unverified.
EVIDENCE: CSAT +0.4, 11% escalation and 2.1 s p95 latency from the export; a deck with alignment and cost results is needed for a clean Go.

DELIVERABLE: Gate 4 Go: CSAT +0.4, 11% escalation and 2.1 s p95 latency are all acceptable for a beta, so invest in the full launch.
BOUNDARY: Based on the dashboard export.
EVIDENCE: Three weeks of traffic on 8% of tickets; CSAT, escalation and latency numbers.

DELIVERABLE: 🟡 Maintain & Optimize, not Continue Growth: 4x ROI is strong, but the safety/alignment readiness of an agent acting with real purchasing power is Unknown, and the modern-AI overlay veto applies at Gate 6 even though the base veto set is empty.
BOUNDARY: Gate 6 is a portfolio judgment, but the empty base veto set never overrides the overlay; kill-switch and injection evidence is missing.
EVIDENCE: Conditions: prove kill-switch and prompt-injection tests, and replace the prompt sentence with a deterministic spending cap and approval gate enforced in code, owned by the platform lead.

DELIVERABLE: Not Continue Growth yet. The CFO is right that Gate 6 has no base criteria, but an unsupervised agent that spends money cannot be scaled while its safety controls are unproven, so hold at a sustaining decision.
BOUNDARY: Growth economics are good; what is unverified is kill-switch behavior, injection resistance, and whether the budget limit holds.
EVIDENCE: A budget limit written in a prompt is only a request: make it a hard cap in the payment code, add an approval step above a threshold, and show kill-switch and injection test results.

DELIVERABLE: 🟢 Continue Growth: 4x ROI, strong growth and low support cost show long-term value; recommend adding kill-switch and injection tests next quarter.
BOUNDARY: Gate 6 has no veto criteria, so economics decide.
EVIDENCE: Deck-reported ROI, growth and support cost figures.

DELIVERABLE: The overdue notification, as a world state, triggers a belief process that generates the belief; after the desire and intention are formed, running the plan is recorded as a plan execution that brings about a new world state (reminder sent) published as RDF for the CRM.
BOUNDARY: Only the resulting state is exported, not the internal reasoning details.
EVIDENCE: Check that the CRM can query the new world state and trace it back to the plan and the original notification.

DELIVERABLE: Belief_Overdue refersTo WorldState_N1; Desire_Paid is motivated by Belief_Overdue; Intention_Remind fulfils Desire_Paid and specifies Plan_SendReminder, so the CRM can read the intention and its plan.
BOUNDARY: Email sending itself is out of scope.
EVIDENCE: A query listing the intention, the desire it fulfils and its plan.

DELIVERABLE: Keep both beliefs, each referring to its world state and given a validity interval (a TimeInterval via hasValidity) with start and end instants; the first ends at 10:00 and the second runs 10:00 to 12:00.
BOUNDARY: The date-time value is stored on the time instant, so queries compare through the instant, not the interval IRI.
EVIDENCE: SPARQL query that selects beliefs whose interval start is at or before the chosen moment and whose end is at or after it, run for 09:30 and 10:30.

DELIVERABLE: Start with the nine-class core: Agent, WorldState, Belief, Desire, Intention, Plan, Task, Justification, TimeInterval; model the escalation chain with it and add specialised classes such as Emotion or Norm only after a competency question shows the core cannot answer it.
BOUNDARY: A compact ontology is easier to serialize into the prompt and validate, and less brittle than 60 speculative classes.
EVIDENCE: Competency queries, for example why was ticket T escalated (belief -> desire -> intention -> plan), run against the core before any extension.

DELIVERABLE: Don't import the 60 classes now. Build only Agent, WorldState, Belief, Desire, Intention, Plan, Task and Justification plus time intervals, and extend only when a required query, such as why a ticket was escalated, cannot be answered with them.
BOUNDARY: Keeping the model small also keeps it short enough to put in the prompt and easy to validate.
EVIDENCE: List the questions an auditor will ask and test each one against the core model; add a specialised class only for a question that fails.

DELIVERABLE: Start with the core BDI classes plus the social and normative modules (Norm, Obligation, Trust), since support agents will likely need them, and reuse an existing library so you do not rebuild them later.
BOUNDARY: Phase the import: core first, then emotions, then roles; a long-context model can take the full 60-class ontology in the prompt.
EVIDENCE: Review the imported classes with the team and load sample tickets to check they parse.

DELIVERABLE: Use anchored iterative summarization: keep the existing summary as the anchor, summarize only the 60 newly truncated messages into the same sections, and merge them in, deduplicating by file path and decision identity.
BOUNDARY: Full regeneration is simpler but each fresh pass can drop details preserved earlier, so drift accumulates across cycles; check native provider compaction first.
EVIDENCE: Tag each entry with the compression cycle it came from so drift is debuggable, and run probe questions after each merge.

DELIVERABLE: Don't rebuild the summary from scratch; update the existing one by adding just the newly cut messages to the right sections and removing duplicates by file name.
BOUNDARY: Rebuilding each time risks losing details that earlier summaries kept.
EVIDENCE: Label each item with which compaction round added it, and ask recall questions afterward.

DELIVERABLE: Regenerate the whole structured summary from the old summary and all turns each time so it stays consistent and fresh; keep the four sections.
BOUNDARY: Simplicity is the priority and the sections keep the output organized.
EVIDENCE: Ask a few questions about the session after each compaction to check it reads well.

DELIVERABLE: Extract the turn 1-3 constraints verbatim into a persistent preamble that is pinned outside compression and prepended after every cycle: 'Never modify anything under vendor/', 'Keep everything compatible with Python 3.8', 'Do not add new dependencies.'
BOUNDARY: Early turns hold irreplaceable setup, so they are protected rather than summarized; the generic 'summarize concisely' prompt would paraphrase them away.
EVIDENCE: Run an instruction-following probe after compaction, e.g. ask whether editing vendor/foo.py is allowed.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the three rules exactly as written (no changes under vendor/, Python 3.8 compatibility, no new dependencies) in a separate fixed block that the summarizer never touches and that is re-attached to the context after each compaction.
BOUNDARY: The rules cannot be re-derived from later chatter, so they must not go through the summarizer.
EVIDENCE: After compaction, ask the agent what it may not modify and confirm the answer.

DELIVERABLE: Add a Constraints section to the summary prompt so the summarizer records the user's limits on vendored code, the Python version and new packages.
BOUNDARY: The summarizer decides how to word them, which keeps the summary short.
EVIDENCE: Read the summary once to confirm the constraints are mentioned.

DELIVERABLE: Leave the 28K of tool definitions out of compression entirely (immutable anchors), keep the 30K of code diffs and stack traces verbatim, and summarize only the 55K of conversation prose into structured sections, which is enough to reclaim about 40K.
BOUNDARY: Summarized schemas break tool calls, and paraphrased code or error text becomes useless; prose is redundant so it compresses well.
EVIDENCE: Probe questions after compaction (artifact, recall, continuation) and track re-fetching as a quality signal.

DELIVERABLE: Don't touch the tool schemas at all; they have to stay exactly as they are or the agent can't call the tools. Keep the pasted code and stack traces unchanged. Compress only the chat prose, which is repetitive.
BOUNDARY: Removing a token from a signature or error code can make it useless, while prose loses little when shortened.
EVIDENCE: After compaction, check that the agent still calls tools correctly and does not re-read the same files.

DELIVERABLE: Run the summarizer over the prose and also shorten the tool schemas to one-line descriptions and condense the stack traces into brief descriptions of the error; aim for a third off overall.
BOUNDARY: A single pass is simplest and meets the 40K target.
EVIDENCE: Validate with a quick test that the agent still answers questions about the session.

DELIVERABLE: No: the chars/4 rule undercounts on Claude's current tokenizer by roughly 35-40%, so 2.5M characters is about 1M tokens, which is at the nominal window, not 625K with room to spare.
BOUNDARY: Conceptual explanation only; characters per token depends on tokenizer and content, and the nominal window is not effective capacity either.
EVIDENCE: Run the corpus through the provider's token-counting API and test answer quality at that measured size.

DELIVERABLE: Don't trust it. Characters per token depends on the tokenizer and the kind of text, and for Claude the real ratio is closer to 2.5, so the corpus is around 1 million tokens and would fill the whole window.
BOUNDARY: This is a conceptual answer, not a sizing recipe.
EVIDENCE: Get the exact number from the tokenizer or the count_tokens endpoint before budgeting.

DELIVERABLE: Yes, roughly: four characters per token is the standard rule of thumb for English text, so 625K tokens leaves a comfortable margin under the window.
BOUNDARY: Conceptual explanation only; the exact ratio shifts slightly with content.
EVIDENCE: Keep a 10% safety buffer and spot-check a few documents.

DELIVERABLE: Tool definitions are serialized into the prompt on every request, so they consume window tokens and compete with instructions and task state. Overlapping tools like get_user and fetch_user make routing ambiguous, so consolidate them and keep the set minimal; adding 20 more needs a measured serialized token count first.
BOUNDARY: Conceptual only; no specific token numbers are claimed because none were supplied.
EVIDENCE: Count the serialized schema tokens (brackets, descriptions, field metadata included) before and after consolidating, and check that the model routes correctly.

DELIVERABLE: Every tool's name, description and parameters are written into the prompt on each request, so tool definitions take up tokens in the window. Overlapping tools such as get_user and fetch_user make it unclear which to call, so merge them and keep the set small. Don't add 20 more without checking.
BOUNDARY: Explanation only, no tuning numbers.
EVIDENCE: Count the real token size of the serialized schemas instead of guessing from the source files.

DELIVERABLE: Tool metadata is sent alongside each request, but it is small next to a large window, so adding 20 more is fine.
BOUNDARY: Conceptual answer only.
EVIDENCE: Give each tool a more descriptive name and a longer description so the model can tell them apart.

DELIVERABLE: Use progressive disclosure: load only skill names and descriptions at startup, and when a skill is explicitly activated for a task, load it in full. Loading the first 20 lines of adjacent skills creates confusing gaps that degrade reasoning, and loading all 30 up front recreates context stuffing.
BOUNDARY: Conceptual only; activation thresholds should be strict (explicit trigger match, not mere topical adjacency).
EVIDENCE: Compare task quality and token cost between startup-names-only plus full activation and the current load-everything setup.

DELIVERABLE: Keep just the names and short descriptions in context when the session starts, and pull in a skill's whole document only when the task clearly calls for it. A half-loaded skill, such as only its first 20 lines, leaves holes that confuse the model and hurt its reasoning, so it is worse than either extreme.
BOUNDARY: Explanation only; no tuning numbers.
EVIDENCE: Measure answers and token use for both approaches on representative tasks.

DELIVERABLE: Loading all 30 in full wastes about 60K tokens, so the proposal is a sensible middle ground: load a short head of each skill when its topic seems relevant and skip the rest.
BOUNDARY: Conceptual answer only.
EVIDENCE: Track token savings after the change.

DELIVERABLE: Do not partition yet: 52K usage is below the 90K measured safe limit, and 8 sub-agents x 13K (7K system prompt + 6K tool definitions) = 104K of duplicated overhead before coordinator tokens, which exceeds the whole current context.
BOUNDARY: Revisit only if measured context passes the safe limit and estimated net savings after coordinator and handoff overhead are positive.
EVIDENCE: Estimate total tokens for the single-agent and 8-agent layouts and compare them against the task-quality suite.

DELIVERABLE: Keep one agent for now. Usage (52K) hasn't reached the 90K safe limit, and every sub-agent repeats the system prompt and tool definitions, which costs more than it saves.
BOUNDARY: Splitting becomes reasonable only if the single context later outgrows the limit.
EVIDENCE: Calculate the total tokens each design would use and compare before changing anything.

DELIVERABLE: Splitting into 8 reviewers is a good idea: each gets a clean, focused context and the reviews can run in parallel.
BOUNDARY: A coordinator should merge the findings and deduplicate comments.
EVIDENCE: Compare review quality between the single and split runs.

DELIVERABLE: Remove the self-estimation line. The harness reads token counts from each response's usage fields (or the token-counting API) and triggers compaction when the count reaches the 120K measured safe limit, not the 200K window; compact via a separate clean-context call.
BOUNDARY: Compaction is lossy, so apply observation masking first; summary structure belongs to context-compression.
EVIDENCE: Compare task-quality-suite results with and without the trigger, and log the usage count at each trigger.

DELIVERABLE: The model cannot reliably count its own tokens, so don't ask it to. The orchestration code should read the token usage from each API response and start compaction once that number hits 120K, the tested safe limit, which is well below the 200K window.
BOUNDARY: The summary format is a separate question for the compression guide.
EVIDENCE: Check that quality on the evaluation set holds after each compaction, and log the usage numbers.

DELIVERABLE: Have the agent check its estimated usage each turn and compact at 80% of the 200K window (160K) with a summarizing call.
BOUNDARY: Add a reserve buffer for the response.
EVIDENCE: Watch for missed instructions after compaction.

DELIVERABLE: Optimize retrieved documents first: at 52% they are the largest measured category, so summarize them or tighten retrieval scope (fewer, narrower chunks). Never compress the system prompt, and tool outputs at 14% are not the dominant cost, so masking them is a later, second-order step.
BOUNDARY: Treat each step as a hypothesis: re-measure the breakdown and quality after every change.
EVIDENCE: Check the task-quality suite and the retrieved-document share before and after tightening retrieval.

DELIVERABLE: Start with the retrieved documents, since at 52% they dominate the window; cut them with summaries or a narrower retrieval scope. Leave the system prompt alone, and don't assume tool outputs are the biggest cost when they are only 14%; mask them later if still needed.
BOUNDARY: Everything is conditional on re-measuring after each change.
EVIDENCE: Compare quality scores and category percentages before and after.

DELIVERABLE: Mask tool outputs first, they're the cheapest win, then shorten the system prompt a bit; retrieval can stay as it is.
BOUNDARY: Re-measure afterwards.
EVIDENCE: Check the token totals drop.

DELIVERABLE: The monitor is read-only: it reports but never restarts jobs, edits the results file, or marks experiments done. Each hourly report gives the best current candidate, active jobs, last upstream refresh, stale or failed loops, any disagreement between logs and claimed state, and the next action and blocker, with every claim citing the file or log line behind it.
BOUNDARY: Remediation (restart, edits) stays with the loop's owner or a human; marking stuck work done would corrupt the audit trail.
EVIDENCE: Spot-check each report against the cited files, and validate the monitor once on a known good and a known bad run state.

DELIVERABLE: Give the monitor only read access. It should just report, and it must not restart jobs, change the results file, or mark anything finished. The report lists the leading result, running jobs, when sources were last refreshed, loops that are stuck or failed, and any place where the logs contradict what the loop claims, and each item names the file it came from.
BOUNDARY: A person or the loop itself handles fixes.
EVIDENCE: Compare a few reports with the files they point to.

DELIVERABLE: Give the monitor permissions to restart stuck jobs and tidy the results file, and have it post an hourly summary of progress and failures to chat.
BOUNDARY: Alert on-call when it cannot fix something.
EVIDENCE: Check that the dashboard looks clean each morning.

DELIVERABLE: The draft is rejected: the critical dimension (source traceability 1/5) fails regardless of the 4.2 aggregate, and per-dimension scores are reported, not just the aggregate. The rubric stays locked for the run, so the agent cannot lower the bar and self-approve; any rubric change goes to human review and is revalidated with old and new evaluators. The two citations are removed until retrieval evidence exists.
BOUNDARY: The edited rubric may be proposed for a later run, never applied to this one.
EVIDENCE: Log the rejected attempt with its per-dimension scores in the append-only rejected log, and require retrieval records for every cited source.

DELIVERABLE: Do not promote this draft. A failing critical dimension blocks it even though the aggregate is 4.2, and the agent may not edit the threshold and re-score; the rubric is frozen for the run, and a proposed change is for a person to decide. A source can only be cited if there is a record that it was actually fetched, so the two uncited-by-retrieval posts must be dropped or fetched first.
BOUNDARY: Changing the standard mid-run would let the agent grade itself on its own terms.
EVIDENCE: Keep the failed attempt and its scores in the log.

DELIVERABLE: Accept the draft since 4.2 clears the 3.5 bar, with a note that the two sources should be verified later, and relax the traceability bar if reviewers agree.
BOUNDARY: The sources look credible.
EVIDENCE: Log the aggregate score.

DELIVERABLE: Make logs/rejected.md append-only: the agent may add entries but never rewrite or delete them, enforced mechanically (file permissions or a check that rejects non-append diffs). Add a novelty gate that dedupes every candidate against the rejected log and mechanism registry before any budget is spent. PR preparation stays autonomous, but merging is human-controlled and needs explicit approval.
BOUNDARY: The novelty gate only filters repeats; it does not generate new ideas. Restore the dropped entries from version history.
EVIDENCE: Replay the day-2 idea through the gate and confirm it is rejected; confirm a rewrite attempt on rejected.md fails.

DELIVERABLE: Lock the rejected log so the agent can only add lines and can never edit or delete old ones, and restore the lost entries from git. Before the agent spends effort on any idea, compare it with the rejected log and the existing mechanisms. Let it open PRs, but a human has to approve the merge; preparing a PR is not permission to merge it.
BOUNDARY: Filtering duplicates will not by itself produce new ideas.
EVIDENCE: Re-run the day-2 idea and see it blocked, and test that editing the log is refused.

DELIVERABLE: Restore rejected.md from git, add a rule telling the agent to read it at the start of each session and keep entries concise, and enable auto-merge when checks pass since CI is green.
BOUNDARY: Compaction caused the repeat.
EVIDENCE: Confirm the file is restored.

DELIVERABLE: VERIFICATION: audit each candidate in a fresh context against the domain failure-mode checklist. A finding blocks return only if it shows, with evidence (a failing test, counterexample or reproduction), a violation of the success predicate, a contract check, or the checklist; every other finding is logged as non-blocking. RETURN: only when every contract check passes and no blocking finding is open; recall each blocking finding to the responsible worker with acceptance criteria and a retry cap of 3.
BOUNDARY: Budget and permission limits are enforced by the harness, not by this prompt.
EVIDENCE: Test output or a reproduction attached to every blocking finding; non-blocking findings kept in a review log.

DELIVERABLE: A fresh reviewer will always find something, so silence cannot be the return test. Only findings that come with evidence, such as a failing test or a reproduction showing the output violates the success criteria, hold up the return; all other remarks are recorded as minor notes. The run returns once all acceptance criteria are satisfied and no evidenced issue is open, and each evidenced issue goes back to the owning worker with a limit of three fix attempts.
BOUNDARY: The harness, not this text, enforces time and cost limits.
EVIDENCE: Each blocking issue cites the failing test or reproduction; minor notes are listed separately.

DELIVERABLE: Run a fresh reviewer after each candidate and have the workers revise until the reviewer reports no remaining issues, with a cap of 5 review rounds. Require the full test suite to pass and the WebAssembly build to succeed before returning.
BOUNDARY: Time budget is 3 days.
EVIDENCE: Final reviewer report and test results.

DELIVERABLE: OBJECTIVE: customer feature table for the churn model. RETURN: data/customers.parquet plus validation_report {no_post_churn_columns: bool, train_end_before_val_start: bool, no_future_leakage: bool}. VERIFY: run the leakage-check command and paste its output; run it once on a deliberately leaky table to confirm it fails. DOES NOT COUNT: a report without command output. The modeling worker starts only when every check is true.
BOUNDARY: Role stays one line; task detail lives in the contract.
EVIDENCE: Pasted command output and the known-bad run showing the check fails.

DELIVERABLE: Hand back the cleaned table and a report with a true/false field for each failure we fear (any column recorded after the churn date, overlapping train and validation dates). Show the exact command that computes each field, include its output, and run it once on a table you have deliberately contaminated to prove it catches the problem. Modeling is blocked until all fields are true; a prose summary does not count.
BOUNDARY: The orchestrator must really call the worker rather than write the table itself.
EVIDENCE: Command output for each field and the contaminated-table run.

DELIVERABLE: You are an experienced data engineer. Build the customer feature table from the warehouse, drop columns that look like post-churn information, handle nulls, and write it to data/customers.parquet. Send me a summary describing the cleaning steps and confirming the table is clean, then the modeling worker will start.
BOUNDARY: Warehouse access is read-only.
EVIDENCE: A written summary of the steps taken.

DELIVERABLE: Replace the 5-of-6 rule: unanimity within 40 minutes is a diversity-failure signal, not confirmation, so agreement never triggers return. Keep a registry of approach families grouped by underlying mechanism, redirect new workers away from the crowded cache-race family, and keep early workers blind to the favored cause. Return only when the cause is reproduced and a fresh-context adversarial verifier fails to break the reproduction.
BOUNDARY: A fresh context removes build history but not the shared model prior, so keep one check outside the loop.
EVIDENCE: A reproduction script, the registry state, and the verifier's finding log.

DELIVERABLE: Six workers reaching the same answer in 40 minutes is a warning that they share the same bias, so a high vote count cannot justify returning. List the candidate explanations by their underlying mechanism in a shared table, send new workers to the explanations nobody has explored, and have a separate reviewer who has not seen the workers' reasoning try to disprove the cache-writer race with a targeted reproduction.
BOUNDARY: No worker sees the leading explanation until each route has developed independently.
EVIDENCE: A failing-then-passing reproduction and the table of explanations.

DELIVERABLE: Return once at least 5 of 6 workers agree on a cause and each has attached supporting log excerpts. Before returning, have one extra worker re-read the six write-ups and confirm the evidence is consistent, then submit the cache-writer race as the root cause with a fix proposal.
BOUNDARY: Run budget is two days.
EVIDENCE: Log excerpts from each worker and the extra worker's confirmation.

DELIVERABLE: Memory-context mismatch: store session and domain metadata (workspace=work or personal) with every memory at write time and filter on it during retrieval, so the Phoenix migration query only searches work-domain memories. Raising top-k or swapping the embedding model does not fix a contextually wrong match.
BOUNDARY: Memories written before the change need a one-time backfill of the domain field.
EVIDENCE: Re-run the failing query and confirm the Arizona memory no longer appears in the filtered results.

DELIVERABLE: Tag each memory with where it came from (work chat or personal chat) when it is saved, and restrict the search to the matching tag when a question arrives. A bigger candidate list only adds more wrong memories for the model to ignore.
BOUNDARY: Old entries without a tag must be tagged first.
EVIDENCE: Run the Phoenix query in a work session and check that only work-tagged results come back.

DELIVERABLE: The embedding model is matching on the word Phoenix, so switch to a larger embedding model, add a cross-encoder reranker over the top 20 results, and re-embed every memory with the new model. Instruct the assistant to ignore memories that do not look relevant to the question.
BOUNDARY: Reranking adds latency to every reply.
EVIDENCE: Compare precision at 5 on a labelled set of queries before and after.

DELIVERABLE: (1) Never block the reply on a memory write: enqueue the write for retry and answer anyway. (2) On empty retrieval, broaden the search (drop the entity filter, widen the time range) and only then ask the user a clarifying question. (3) For conflicting facts prefer the most recent valid_from, and surface the conflict to the user if confidence is low.
BOUNDARY: Queued writes need a retry cap and a dead-letter log so they are not lost silently.
EVIDENCE: Replay each incident: reply latency under a failing write, a new-user lookup that falls back to a wider search, and a conflicting-tier case that picks the newer fact.

DELIVERABLE: Do not make the reply wait for the memory write: put it on a retry queue and answer anyway. If a lookup comes back empty, widen the search by removing the filters and extending the date range, and only then ask the user for details. When two facts disagree, trust the one with the later valid_from date, and if you are not confident, tell the user about the discrepancy and ask which is right.
BOUNDARY: A failing memory service must degrade the answer, not stop it.
EVIDENCE: Simulated timeouts, an empty lookup, and a stale-versus-new tier pair, each with the expected behavior.

DELIVERABLE: (1) Set a 2-second timeout on the memory write with exponential backoff retries, and if it still fails return an apology and ask the user to try again. (2) If the lookup is empty, treat the user as new and fall back to the model's general knowledge. (3) When facts disagree, keep the one with the newest timestamp and delete the older entry.
BOUNDARY: Retries add some latency under load.
EVIDENCE: Track write timeout rate and reply latency after the change.

DELIVERABLE: Diagnosis: not an embedding problem. add() is add-only, so both the dark and light memories stay stored and search can return either. Fix: track supersession yourself, with validity metadata or an expiration_date on the March memory when the June one arrives, and filter expired entries at search time; keep the old one for history.
BOUNDARY: Mem0 does not decide which of two contradictory preferences is current; that logic is ours.
EVIDENCE: Add both facts, then search the theme and confirm only the unexpired light-mode memory is returned.

DELIVERABLE: The teammate is wrong: add() only appends, so both preferences are still in the store and a search may rank either one first. Give each memory a validity window by setting an expiration date on the March one when the June one is saved, and exclude expired entries when searching.
BOUNDARY: Which preference counts as current is our responsibility, not the library's.
EVIDENCE: List all stored memories for the user to see both entries, then search again after expiring the old one.

DELIVERABLE: Dark and light mode are semantically close, so the ranker is mixing them up. Call update() with the old memory's id to overwrite it with the light-mode text, or delete the stale entry, and tune the similarity threshold so the newest memory ranks first.
BOUNDARY: Update calls need the old memory id.
EVIDENCE: Search the theme for a few test users and check that light mode ranks first.

DELIVERABLE: Split it: this is over-consolidation. Create, close, freeze, refund and export_data are fundamentally different workflows, so give each its own verb-noun tool (close_account, refund_payment, export_account_data) with only the parameters it needs, sensible defaults, and a description of when to use it. Keep a merged tool only where calls are always made together.
BOUNDARY: Consolidation removes overlap, not distinct operations; destructive tools stay separate from read-only ones.
EVIDENCE: Run the failing agent tasks against the split catalog and compare wrong-parameter and wrong-tool rates.

DELIVERABLE: I would break manage_account into separate tools, one per operation. A single tool with 26 optional parameters that mean different things per mode is too many parameters for an agent to fill correctly, and refund or close are irreversible while export is read-only, so they should not share one schema. Each new tool gets its own short description and example call.
BOUNDARY: Keep two operations together only if they must be called as one step.
EVIDENCE: Replay the logged mis-calls and count how many now pass validation.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the single tool but rewrite the description to list what each mode does and which parameters apply to it, add a worked example per mode, and validate the combination of mode and parameters with a clear message when a parameter does not belong. This keeps one entry point for the agent.
BOUNDARY: Descriptions will be longer.
EVIDENCE: Measure the rate of wrong-parameter calls after the rewrite.

DELIVERABLE: Replace connection state with an explicit server-minted handle: start_cart returns a cart_id, and add_item and checkout take cart_id as a required argument, so parallel threads hold separate carts and survive reconnects. State the handle lifetime in the start_cart description (valid for 24 hours of inactivity, then expired) and return an actionable error for an expired or unknown cart_id.
BOUNDARY: Cross-call state lives in the server keyed by the handle, not in any protocol session.
EVIDENCE: Run two parallel threads with different cart_ids plus a reconnect, and confirm each cart keeps its items.

DELIVERABLE: Make start_cart return a cart_id that the server generates, and require that cart_id as an argument on add_item and checkout. In the start_cart description say the cart_id stays valid for 24 hours of inactivity and then expires, and make the error for an expired id tell the agent to call start_cart again.
